study.title: Soil Inorganic Electron Acceptors and Carbon Substrates Hierarchically Govern Wetland Methanogenesis Temperature Response

cover.headline: The temperature sensitivity of methane from wetlands depends less on climate, **more on what's in the soil**.

slides.title: Wetlands are Earth's largest natural methane source, but we can't predict how they'll respond to warming.
slides.body:
Climate models need to know how fast wetland microbes will make methane as temperatures rise. That rate varies wildly across different wetlands, but no one knew why. The assumption was climate or water levels would explain the difference.

The puzzle: identical wetlands in similar climates can show temperature sensitivities that differ sevenfold. Something else was controlling the response.

slides.title: Temperature sensitivity varied up to sevenfold across wetlands, driven by soil chemistry rather than climate.
slides.body:
Across 276 soil samples from 69 wetlands, the temperature sensitivity of methane production ranged from 1.12 to 7.75. Climate factors explained none of that variation.

Instead, two soil properties controlled it hierarchically. Inorganic electron acceptors in the soil dampened temperature sensitivity through thermodynamic constraints. Carbon-to-nitrogen ratio only mattered when those electron acceptors were low enough to release the thermodynamic brake.

slides.title: Predicting wetland methane feedback to climate requires mapping soil chemistry, not just temperature or water.
slides.body:
Current climate models treat wetland methane as a function of temperature and hydrology. This study shows the intrinsic biogeochemical state of the soil determines how much warming actually increases methane emissions.

That means continental-scale predictions need detailed soil chemistry data. Two wetlands at the same latitude with identical water tables could respond completely differently to the same warming, depending on what's dissolved in their soils.

caveats: This study measured potential methane production in controlled lab incubations, not emissions from intact wetlands in the field.
The hierarchical control framework was identified through correlation across diverse sites, not through experimental manipulation of soil chemistry.

cta.headline: How soil chemistry throttles warming
cta.sub: The biogeochemical details that determine which wetlands will amplify climate change.

caption: Whether a wetland becomes a methane bomb under warming turns out to depend less on how hot it gets and more on what's already in the soil. Researchers analyzed 276 soil samples from 69 wetlands and found temperature sensitivity ranging from 1.12 to 7.75, with soil electron acceptors acting as the primary brake and carbon quality as a conditional accelerator. The study used lab incubations to isolate microbial methanogenesis from field complexities. This suggests wetland climate models need a chemistry overhaul, not just better temperature maps. Full study: doi.org/10.1002/advs.202518281 — Biggest wetland near you?

unsupported_claims.claim: Temperature sensitivity varied up to sevenfold across wetlands
unsupported_claims.problem: The abstract states the range was 1.12-7.75, which represents approximately a 6.9-fold difference (7.75/1.12 = 6.92), not 'up to sevenfold'. However, 'sevenfold' is a reasonable simplification for lay communication.
Same as above - the exact range yields 6.9-fold. This is a minor rounding/simplification.

unsupported_claims.claim: identical wetlands in similar climates can show temperature sensitivities that differ sevenfold
unsupported_claims.problem: The abstract does not mention 'identical wetlands in similar climates' - it states Q10-CH4 varies independent of climatic factors, but doesn't describe comparing identical wetlands

unsupported_claims.claim: That means continental-scale predictions need detailed soil chemistry data
unsupported_claims.problem: While the abstract mentions 'continental scales' in the context of understanding influences on Q10-CH4, it does not explicitly state that predictions 'need' detailed soil chemistry data - this is an inference/interpretation

unsupported_claims.claim: Whether a wetland becomes a methane bomb under warming
unsupported_claims.problem: The phrase 'methane bomb' is not in the abstract and represents editorializing/dramatization beyond what the study claims

unsupported_claims.claim: The study used lab incubations to isolate microbial methanogenesis from field complexities
unsupported_claims.problem: While the copy correctly notes these were lab incubations in the disclaimer, this specific framing about 'isolating from field complexities' is not stated in the abstract
